zhou-dynasty.name: Zhou dynasty
zhou-dynasty.summary: A Chinese royal dynasty that ruled for 790 years, roughly 1046 to 256 BC, the longest of any Chinese dynasty, its power fading before Qin conquered it.

qin-shi-huang.name: Qin Shi Huang
qin-shi-huang.summary: First emperor of a unified China (259 to 210 BC), founder of the Qin dynasty, who standardized reforms and linked earlier walls into a single Great Wall.

qin-dynasty.name: Qin dynasty
qin-dynasty.summary: First imperial dynasty of China, founded in 221 BCE when King Ying Zheng unified the warring states; it lasted only 14 years but its administrative system shaped later Chinese dynasties.

han-dynasty.name: Han dynasty
han-dynasty.summary: An imperial Chinese dynasty (202 BC–220 AD) seen as a golden age of Chinese history; the majority Chinese ethnic group, language and script are named after it.

i-ching.name: I Ching
i-ching.summary: Ancient Chinese divination text, also called the Book of Changes, that evolved into a philosophical work central to Confucian, Taoist and Buddhist thought and later influenced Western ideas.

xi-an.name: Xi'an
xi-an.summary: Capital of Shaanxi province and one of China's oldest cities, long known as Chang'an and a capital under dynasties including the Han and Tang; home to the Terracotta Army.

shaanxi.name: Shaanxi
shaanxi.summary: A province in Northwestern China covering over 205,000 square kilometres, home to Xi'an, one of China's oldest cities and capital of several ancient dynasties.

bi-jade.name: Bi
bi-jade.summary: A circular ancient Chinese jade artifact, first produced in the Neolithic Liangzhu culture (3400 to 2250 BCE) and later mainly during the Shang, Zhou and Han dynasties.

xu-shen.name: Xu Shen
xu-shen.summary: Chinese calligrapher, philologist and scholar (c. 58–148 CE) of the Eastern Han dynasty, best known for writing the Shuowen Jiezi, the first comprehensive Chinese character dictionary.

oracle-bone-script.name: Oracle bone script
oracle-bone-script.summary: Oldest known form of written Chinese, carved into bones and shells to record royal divinations for the Late Shang court; most surviving examples come from the last Shang capital near modern Anyang.

chinese-bronze-inscriptions.name: Bronzeware script
chinese-bronze-inscriptions.summary: Chinese writing cast or engraved on ritual bronzes mainly during the Late Shang and Western Zhou dynasties (about 1250-771 BC), one of the earliest scripts in the Chinese writing family.

cai-lun.name: Cai Lun
cai-lun.summary: A Chinese court official of the Eastern Han dynasty traditionally credited with improving papermaking by adding pulp from bark and hemp.

sumatran-rhinoceros.name: Sumatran rhinoceros
sumatran-rhinoceros.summary: The smallest living rhinoceros species, with two horns and reddish-brown hair, once found from India to China but now critically endangered with fewer than 80 wild individuals left.

shang-dynasty.name: Shang dynasty
shang-dynasty.summary: A Chinese royal dynasty that ruled the Yellow River valley in the 2nd millennium BCE, the earliest Chinese dynasty confirmed by archaeology, known for oracle-bone writing found at its capital near Anyang.

palaeoloxodon.name: Palaeoloxodon
palaeoloxodon.summary: An extinct elephant genus that spread from Africa into Eurasia, including some of the largest land mammals ever known and, on Mediterranean islands, some of the smallest elephants.

rammed-earth.name: Hangtu
rammed-earth.summary: An ancient technique of compacting layers of earth, chalk, lime or gravel to build walls, floors and foundations, used worldwide and for millennia in China.

wuwei-gansu.name: Wuwei, Gansu
wuwei-gansu.summary: City in northwest China's Gansu province, a key business and transportation hub along the Hexi Corridor that historically linked central China to Central Asia.

elasmotherium.name: Elasmotherium
elasmotherium.summary: An extinct genus of giant rhinoceros that lived across Eastern Europe, Central Asia and East Asia until at least 39,000 years ago, reaching sizes comparable to an elephant.

qilin.name: Qilin
qilin.summary: A legendary hooved creature in Chinese mythology, said to appear before the arrival or death of a great sage or ruler.

spring-and-autumn-period.name: Spring and Autumn period
spring-and-autumn-period.summary: A period of Chinese history, about 770 to 481 BCE, marked by declining Zhou royal power as local lords gained growing autonomy, named after its chronicle.

battle-of-muye.name: Battle of Muye
battle-of-muye.summary: A battle around 1046 BC in which the rebel Zhou state under King Wu defeated the Shang dynasty, ending Shang rule and founding the Zhou dynasty.

the-art-of-war.name: The Art of War
the-art-of-war.summary: An ancient Chinese military treatise from around the 5th century BCE, attributed to Sun Tzu, covering strategy, logistics, morale and espionage, and hugely influential on military thinking.

sun-tzu.name: Sun Tzu
sun-tzu.summary: A Chinese general, strategist and philosopher of the Eastern Zhou period, traditionally credited as the author of The Art of War, though parts of the text likely date from after his lifetime.

warring-states-period.name: Warring States period
warring-states-period.summary: A Chinese era from about 475 to 221 BC marked by intense warfare and political consolidation, ending when the state of Qin conquered its rivals and founded the first imperial dynasty.

qin-state.name: Qin (state)
qin-state.summary: An ancient Chinese state of the Zhou dynasty, traditionally dated from 897 BC, that unified China's Seven Warring States under Qin Shi Huang in 221 BC.

wei-qing.name: Wei Qing
wei-qing.summary: Chinese general and politician of the Western Han dynasty (died c. 106 BC), acclaimed for his campaigns against the Xiongnu and his rise from humble origins.

battle-of-mobei.name: Battle of Mobei
battle-of-mobei.summary: A January 119 BC campaign in the Gobi Desert in which Han dynasty forces under Wei Qing and Huo Qubing defeated the nomadic Xiongnu, reaching as far as Lake Baikal.

xiongnu.name: Xiongnu
xiongnu.summary: A nomadic tribal confederation dominating the eastern Eurasian steppe from the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD, founded as an empire by Modu Chanyu, eventually defeated by the Han dynasty.

chanyu.name: Chanyu
chanyu.summary: Title used for eight centuries by supreme rulers of Inner Asian nomads, most famously the Xiongnu, until replaced by "Khagan" in 402 AD.

chu-state.name: Chu
chu-state.summary: An ancient Chinese state of the Zhou dynasty, founded in the early 8th century BC south of the Zhou heartland, annexed by Qin in 223 BC.

wu-state.name: Wu
wu-state.summary: An ancient Chinese state at the mouth of the Yangtze River during the Western Zhou dynasty and Spring and Autumn period, located east of Chu and south of Qi.

quanrong.name: Quanrong
quanrong.summary: Ancient ethnic group known as the "Dog Rong," active in northwestern China during and after the Zhou dynasty, sometimes clashing with Chinese states along their frontiers.

ba-state.name: Ba
ba-state.summary: An ancient state in eastern Sichuan formed of loosely affiliated clans who relied on fishing and hunting rather than farming, conquered by the state of Qin in 316 BC.

shu-kingdom.name: Shu (kingdom)
shu-kingdom.summary: An ancient kingdom based on the Chengdu Plain in what is now Sichuan, China, conquered by the state of Qin in 316 BC; the region kept the name Shu afterward.

yinqueshan-han-slips.name: Yinqueshan Han Slips
yinqueshan-han-slips.summary: Bamboo writing tablets from the Western Han dynasty, discovered in 1972 near Linyi, Shandong, containing previously unknown or newly clarified ancient texts.

linyi.name: Linyi
linyi.summary: A prefecture-level city in Shandong, China, the province's largest by area and population as of 2011, whose name means 'close to the Yi River'.

sun-bin.name: Sun Bin
sun-bin.summary: A Chinese military strategist of the Warring States period (382–316 BCE), said to descend from Sun Tzu, who was crippled by a rival before becoming a celebrated commander for the state of Qi.

hangu-pass.name: Hangu Pass
hangu-pass.summary: A fortified mountain pass built by the state of Qin in 330 BC that guarded the main route between the Central Plain and the Guanzhong region.

wei-state.name: Wei (state)
wei-state.summary: One of the seven major Warring States of ancient China, created from the Partition of Jin alongside Han and Zhao, lying between the states of Qin and Qi.

classic-of-poetry.name: Classic of Poetry
classic-of-poetry.summary: The oldest surviving collection of Chinese poetry, comprising 305 works from the 11th to 7th centuries BC and traditionally said to be edited by Confucius.

chengyu.name: Chengyu
chengyu.summary: Traditional four-character Chinese idiomatic expressions, numbering roughly 5,000 by the strictest definition, regarded as carrying the collected wisdom and moral lessons of past generations.

chu-ci.name: Chu Ci
chu-ci.summary: An ancient anthology of Chinese poetry mainly attributed to Qu Yuan and Song Yu, compiled in its traditional 17-section form by the 2nd-century librarian Wang Yi.

qu-yuan.name: Qu Yuan
qu-yuan.summary: Chinese poet and political figure of the State of Chu (c. 340–278 BC), central figure of the Chu Ci poetry anthology, later linked to the Dragon Boat Festival through his death by drowning.

song-yu.name: Song Yu
song-yu.summary: Chinese poet of the late Warring States period (active 298–263 BCE), traditionally credited as author of several poems in the Verses of Chu.

sima-qian.name: Sima Qian
sima-qian.summary: Chinese historian of the early Han dynasty, c. 145–86 BC, considered the father of Chinese historiography for the Shiji, spanning over two thousand years of history.

shiji.name: Shiji
shiji.summary: A Chinese historical text written in the late 2nd and early 1st centuries BC by Han dynasty historian Sima Qian, covering 2,500 years of history and setting the model for all later Chinese dynastic histories.

li-si.name: Li Si
li-si.summary: Chinese calligrapher, philosopher, and Qin dynasty chancellor (c. 280–208 BC) who helped unify China's laws, measures, and writing after Qin Shi Huang's conquest.

confucius.name: Confucius
confucius.summary: Chinese philosopher (c. 551–479 BCE) whose teachings on morality, family loyalty, and social harmony, known as Confucianism, shaped much of Chinese and East Asian culture.

zuo-zhuan.name: Zuo Zhuan
zuo-zhuan.summary: An ancient Chinese narrative history covering 722 to 468 BC, traditionally a commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals, long the primary text through which educated Chinese learned their ancient history.

liu-xiang-scholar.name: Liu Xiang
liu-xiang-scholar.summary: A Chinese astronomer, historian, librarian, poet and politician of the Western Han dynasty (77-6 BCE), known for cataloguing and editing the imperial library.

classic-of-mountains-and-seas.name: Classic of Mountains and Seas
classic-of-mountains-and-seas.summary: A Chinese classic compiling mythic geography and creatures, tracing to the 4th century BCE, describing over 550 mountains and 300 waterways.

biographies-of-exemplary-women.name: Biographies of Exemplary Women
biographies-of-exemplary-women.summary: A book compiled around 18 BCE by Han dynasty scholar Liu Xiang, containing 125 biographical accounts of exemplary women in ancient China and used for two millennia as a standard text on women's moral education.

nine-laments.name: Nine Laments
nine-laments.summary: One of 17 major sections of the ancient Chinese poetry collection Chu Ci, made up of nine verses each paired with a concluding lament, attributed to Liu Xiang.

zuo-qiuming.name: Zuo Qiuming
zuo-qiuming.summary: Chinese historian and contemporary of Confucius in the Lu state, traditionally credited with the Zuo Zhuan and Guoyu, and said by some accounts to have been blind.

book-of-documents.name: Book of Documents
book-of-documents.summary: One of the Five Classics of ancient Chinese literature, a collection of rhetorical prose that formed the foundation of Chinese political philosophy for over two thousand years.

bamboo-texts-of-guodian.name: Guodian Chu Slips
bamboo-texts-of-guodian.summary: A corpus of bamboo-strip manuscripts unearthed in 1993 from a tomb in Jingmen, Hubei Province, dated to the latter half of China's Warring States period.

gushi-poetry.name: Gushi
gushi-poetry.summary: A classical Chinese poetry form meaning 'old-style poetry,' referring to certain early exemplary poems and later works written in the same style.

mao-heng.name: Mao Heng
mao-heng.summary: A Confucian scholar of the Warring States or early Han period, known for his annotations to the Classic of Poetry.

emperor-ping-of-han.name: Emperor Ping of Han
emperor-ping-of-han.summary: Eleventh emperor of China's Han dynasty, reigning from age eight (1 BC to AD 6) under regent Wang Mang, who allegedly poisoned him as real Han power ended.

zheng-xuan.name: Zheng Xuan
zheng-xuan.summary: Chinese philosopher, politician and writer (127–200) at the end of the Eastern Han dynasty, a student of Ma Rong known for his scholarly annotated editions of classical texts.

fu-poetry.name: Fu (poetry)
fu-poetry.summary: A Chinese rhymed prose form dominant during the Han dynasty (206 BC-AD 220), rhapsodizing a subject in exhaustive detail between poetry and prose.

six-dynasties.name: Six Dynasties
six-dynasties.summary: A collective term for six Han-ruled Chinese dynasties from the early 3rd to late 6th century AD, between the Eastern Han and the Sui dynasty.

erya.name: Erya
erya.summary: The earliest surviving Chinese dictionary, with entries believed to mostly date from the 3rd century BCE.

fangyan-book.name: Fangyan
fangyan-book.summary: An early Chinese dictionary compiled by poet and philosopher Yang Xiong in the early 1st century CE, notable as the first to include significant regional vocabulary.

shuowen-jiezi.name: Shuowen Jiezi
shuowen-jiezi.summary: Chinese dictionary compiled by Xu Shen around 100 CE, the first to comprehensively analyze characters by their structure and organize them by shared radicals.

bamboo-annals.name: Bamboo Annals
bamboo-annals.summary: A chronicle of ancient China running from legendary times to 299 BC, focused later on the State of Wei, surviving today in two disputed versions after the original was possibly lost.

anyang.name: Anyang
anyang.summary: A city in Henan, China, and site of the ancient capital of Yin, the first stable capital of the Shang dynasty and one of the birthplaces of Chinese civilization.

wu-ding.name: Wu Ding
wu-ding.summary: King of the Shang dynasty who died around 1192 BC; oracle bone inscriptions from his reign, unearthed in 1899, are the earliest confirmed Chinese writing and make up over half of all known Shang inscriptions.

lunar-station.name: Lunar mansion
lunar-station.summary: A segment of the ecliptic the Moon passes through in its orbit, used by several ancient cultures, including China, as part of their calendar systems.

joseph-needham.name: Joseph Needham
joseph-needham.summary: British biochemist, historian of science and sinologist known for the multivolume Science and Civilisation in China and for posing the "Needham Question" about China's loss of scientific leadership.

armillary-sphere.name: Armillary sphere
armillary-sphere.summary: Model of the celestial sphere made of rings representing lines such as the ecliptic, invented separately in ancient China and Greece and later used in the Islamic world and medieval Europe.

fu-an.name: Fu An
fu-an.summary: Ming dynasty diplomat (active 1395-1429) sent on missions across Central Asia, imprisoned in Samarkand by Timur until 1407.

zhang-heng.name: Zhang Heng
zhang-heng.summary: Chinese polymath of the Eastern Han dynasty (78–139) who served as Chief Astronomer and invented the world's first water-powered armillary sphere and first seismoscope.

shi-shen.name: Shi Shen
shi-shen.summary: A Chinese astronomer and astrologer active in the 4th century BCE, from the State of Wei.

divination-by-astrological-and-meteorolo.name: Divination by Astrological and Meteorological Phenomena
divination-by-astrological-and-meteorolo.summary: Ancient Chinese silk manuscript found at Mawangdui in 1973, listing 29 comets ('broom stars') that appeared over about 300 years, with accompanying drawings.
divination-by-astrological-and-meteorolo.source_title: Divination by Astrological and Meteorological Phenomena

water-clock.name: Clepsydra
water-clock.summary: An ancient timepiece that measures time by the regulated flow of water, used in Babylon, Egypt and Persia from around the 16th century BC and later in Greece and Rome.

luoxia-hong.name: Luoxia Hong
luoxia-hong.summary: A Chinese astronomer of the Western Han dynasty (c. 130-70 BCE) who helped create the Tai Chu calendar adopted in 104 BCE, using an armillary sphere he improved or invented.

archimedes.name: Archimedes
archimedes.summary: Ancient Greek mathematician, physicist and engineer from Syracuse (c. 287–212 BC), regarded as one of the greatest mathematicians of all time for his work on geometry, levers and buoyancy.

hero-of-alexandria.name: Hero of Alexandria
hero-of-alexandria.summary: Greek mathematician and engineer active in Roman-era Alexandria, seen as antiquity's greatest experimentalist; invented the steam-powered aeolipile and an early windwheel, and gave Heron's formula for triangle area.

shen-kuo.name: Shen Kuo
shen-kuo.summary: Chinese polymath, scientist and statesman of the Northern Song dynasty (1031–1095), first to describe the magnetic needle compass in his 1088 essays.

tomb-of-marquis-yi-of-zeng.name: Tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng
tomb-of-marquis-yi-of-zeng.summary: An intact royal tomb from around 433 BCE in Hubei, China, holding the remains of Marquis Yi of the state of Zeng along with ritual bronzes and a famous set of bells.
tomb-of-marquis-yi-of-zeng.source_title: Tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng

twenty-eight-mansions.name: Twenty-Eight Mansions
twenty-eight-mansions.summary: A system of Chinese constellations tracking the Moon's path across the sky roughly one mansion per day, also used in Japan and paralleled by India's nakshatra system.

mawangdui-silk-texts.name: Mawangdui Silk Texts
mawangdui-silk-texts.summary: Chinese philosophical and medical writings on silk, discovered in 1973 at Changsha and dating to before 168 BCE, including some of the earliest known copies of the I Ching and Tao Te Ching.

mandate-of-heaven.name: Mandate of Heaven
mandate-of-heaven.summary: A Chinese political doctrine legitimizing rulers as chosen by Heaven, with loss of virtue or disasters seen as signs a dynasty should be overthrown.

huaxia.name: Huaxia
huaxia.summary: A historical concept of shared cultural ancestry among the Han Chinese, first attested before 300 BCE, denoting a confederation of Yellow River tribes seen as their ancestors.

king-wu-of-zhou.name: King Wu of Zhou
king-wu-of-zhou.summary: Founding king of China's Zhou dynasty, died around 1043 BC; in 1046 BC he defeated the Shang dynasty at the Battle of Muye, ending Shang rule and beginning the Zhou era.

spring-and-autumn-annals.name: Spring and Autumn Annals
spring-and-autumn-annals.summary: An ancient Chinese chronicle of the State of Lu covering 722 to 481 BCE, traditionally attributed to Confucius and counted among the Five Classics.

emperor-wu-of-han.name: Emperor Wu of Han
emperor-wu-of-han.summary: Seventh emperor of the Han dynasty, reigning from 141 to 87 BCE for 54 years, a record among Han emperors. His rule brought vast territorial expansion, a centralized state, and increased contact with western Eurasia.

baiyue.name: Baiyue
baiyue.summary: Various ethnic groups living across southern China and northern Vietnam during the 1st millennia BC and AD, known for short hair, tattoos and skilled seafaring, later assimilated into Chinese culture.

minyue.name: Minyue
minyue.summary: An ancient kingdom in what is now Fujian, China, contemporary with the Han dynasty, existing from about 306 BC until its annexation by Han in 110 BC.

nanyue.name: Nanyue
nanyue.summary: An ancient kingdom founded in 204 BC by the Chinese general Zhao Tuo, covering parts of modern southern China and northern Vietnam, conquered by the Han dynasty in 111 BC.

dian-kingdom.name: Dian
dian-kingdom.summary: An ancient kingdom of the non-Han Dian people around Dian Lake in Yunnan, China, from at least the 8th century BCE until annexed by the Han Empire in 109 BCE.

emperor-guangwu-of-han.name: Emperor Guangwu of Han
emperor-guangwu-of-han.summary: Founding emperor of China's Eastern Han dynasty (5 BC–AD 57), who reunified China by 36 CE after civil war and made Taoism the dynasty's official religion.

luoyang.name: Luoyang
luoyang.summary: A city in Henan province, China, among the oldest in the country and the earliest of its Four Great Ancient Capitals, at the meeting of the Luo and Yellow rivers.

ban-chao.name: Ban Chao
ban-chao.summary: A Chinese diplomat, explorer and Han-dynasty general (32–102 CE) who governed Central Asia's Western Regions, fought the Xiongnu for over 30 years and restored Han control over the Tarim Basin.

pamir-mountains.name: Pamir Mountains
pamir-mountains.summary: A mountain range in Central and South Asia where the Tian Shan, Karakoram, Kunlun, Hindu Kush and Himalayas meet, known since Victorian times as the 'Roof of the World.'

wang-mang.name: Wang Mang
wang-mang.summary: Founder and only emperor of China's short-lived Xin dynasty, who seized the Han throne in 9 AD, abolished slavery, redistributed land, and was killed in 23 AD when rebels overran his capital.

gan-ying.name: Gan Ying
gan-ying.summary: A Chinese diplomat sent in 97 CE by the general Ban Chao to learn about the Roman Empire, who turned back after reaching a 'western sea' well short of Rome.

kushan-empire.name: Kushan Empire
kushan-empire.summary: A syncretic empire (c. 30–375 CE) formed by the Yuezhi, spreading from Bactria across what is now Afghanistan, Pakistan and northern India; its rulers patronized Buddhism and helped spread it into Central Asia and China.

emperor-wu-of-jin.name: Sima Yan
emperor-wu-of-jin.summary: First emperor of the Jin dynasty, reigning 266 to 290, who reunified China by conquering the state of Eastern Wu in 280. Known for generosity but also extravagance, he empowered royal relatives, later destabilizing the dynasty.

jin-dynasty-266-420.name: Jin dynasty
jin-dynasty-266-420.summary: Chinese dynasty (266–420 CE) founded by Sima Yan; its Western phase collapsed under invasion in 316, continuing afterward as the Eastern Jin in the south.

king-nan-of-zhou.name: King Nan of Zhou
king-nan-of-zhou.summary: The last king of China's Zhou dynasty, reigning from 314 to 256 BC — the longest reign of the dynasty — though by then holding little real political power.

mencius.name: Mencius
mencius.summary: A Chinese Confucian philosopher (c. 371–289 BC), called the 'Second Sage', who taught that human nature is fundamentally good, unlike his contemporary Xunzi.

mozi.name: Mozi
mozi.summary: A Chinese philosopher and logician of the Warring States period (c. 475–221 BCE) who founded Mohism, a school teaching universal love, social order and honoring the worthy.

han-fei.name: Han Fei
han-fei.summary: A Chinese Legalist philosopher and statesman of the Warring States period (c. 280–233 BC), often considered Legalism's greatest representative through the writings later collected as the Han Feizi.

xunzi-philosopher.name: Xunzi
xunzi-philosopher.summary: Confucian philosopher of the late Warring States period (c. 310 – after 238 BCE), often ranked third after Confucius and Mencius, who synthesized rival schools of thought into Confucianism.

wuxing-chinese-philosophy.name: Wuxing
wuxing-chinese-philosophy.summary: Chinese philosophical scheme of five phases-Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal and Water-formalized under the Han dynasty and used to explain cycles in medicine, politics and religion.

xuanxue.name: Xuanxue
xuanxue.summary: A metaphysical Chinese philosophy of the Six Dynasties period (222–589) that blended Taoist and Confucian ideas, sometimes called Neo-Taoism.

hundred-schools-of-thought.name: Hundred Schools of Thought
hundred-schools-of-thought.summary: The flourishing of rival Chinese philosophies, including Confucianism, Mohism and Legalism, during the turbulent Warring States period (c. 500-221 BCE), ended by the Qin dynasty's suppression of scholars.

legalism-chinese-philosophy.name: Legalism
legalism-chinese-philosophy.summary: A Chinese political philosophy from the Warring States period holding that people are self-interested, favoring strict laws, meritocracy, and strong agriculture and military over aristocratic power.

mixed-school-chinese-philosophy.name: Zajia
mixed-school-chinese-philosophy.summary: An eclectic school of thought in Chinese philosophy combining Confucianism, Taoism, Mohism and Legalism, known through texts like the Lüshi Chunqiu; the label was applied later.

shizi-book.name: Shizi
shizi-book.summary: An eclectic Chinese philosophical text written around 330 BCE by Shi Jiao, blending Confucian, Daoist, Mohist and Legalist ideas; most of it was later lost and only partly reconstructed.

l-shi-chunqiu.name: Lüshi Chunqiu
l-shi-chunqiu.summary: Encyclopedic Chinese classic compiled around 239 BC under Qin chancellor Lü Buwei, drawing on many philosophical traditions and covering topics like music and agriculture.

huainanzi.name: Huainanzi
huainanzi.summary: An ancient Chinese philosophical and governmental text compiled from scholarly debates before 139 BCE, blending Taoist, Legalist, Confucian and Mohist ideas.

wu-wei.name: Wu wei
wu-wei.summary: Ancient Chinese philosophical concept of effortless, unforced action, central to Taoism's idea of flowing with nature and later applied to an ideal, hands-off style of rule.

shangdi.name: Shangdi
shangdi.summary: The name for the Chinese "Lord Above," the highest deity in classical Chinese theology, rooted in Shang-dynasty worship and still used today in several Chinese religious and philosophical traditions.

n-wa.name: Nüwa
n-wa.summary: A mother goddess and creator figure in Chinese mythology, credited with shaping humanity from clay and repairing the pillars of Heaven; one of the most venerated goddesses in Chinese culture.

huang-lao.name: Huang-Lao
huang-lao.summary: The most influential school of Chinese thought in the early Han dynasty, blending political philosophy with the origins of religious Taoism.

houmuwu-ding.name: Houmuwu Ding
houmuwu-ding.summary: A rectangular bronze ritual vessel of China's Shang dynasty, the heaviest surviving bronze from the ancient world, unearthed in 1939 near the last Shang capital at Anyang.

taotie.name: Taotie
taotie.summary: An ancient Chinese mythological creature commonly shown as a mask-like motif on bronze ritual vessels during the Shang and Zhou dynasties.

queen-mother-of-the-west.name: Queen Mother of the West
queen-mother-of-the-west.summary: A mother goddess in Chinese religion and mythology, attested since Shang dynasty oracle-bone inscriptions and closely tied to Taoism; her cult, promising prosperity, longevity and bliss, grew especially under the Han dynasty.
